groups.text: This Kotlin suspend function waits twice: for the card vault, then for the issuer.
Java has no suspend, so this is Kotlin only.
While it waits, it holds no thread.
How can a function stop in the middle and carry on later?
The J V M has no special support for coroutines.
The Kotlin compiler rewrites the function.
It adds a hidden last parameter, a Continuation, and changes the return type to Object.
It returns the real result, or a marker, COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, which means: I paused, I will call you back.
Then it cuts the body at each suspension point.
Two suspending calls give three states: label zero, one and two.
The state lives in one small object on the heap: the label, and every local that must survive a pause.
Run it on a pool of threads.
worker-one starts at label zero.
It saves pan in the object, sets the label to one, and calls tokenize.
tokenize must wait for the vault, so it returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, and chargeCard passes the marker straight up the stack.
worker-one is now free, and goes back to the pool to run other coroutines.
This payment holds no thread, only the object.
The vault answers.
The dispatcher resumes the coroutine on whatever pool thread is free: this time, worker-three.
resumeWith calls chargeCard again with the same object, and a switch on the label jumps to label one.
It keeps the token in the object, sets the label to two, and calls authorize.
That suspends too, and worker-three leaves.
When the issuer answers, worker-two resumes it at label two, and it returns the result.
If a call does not need to wait, say on a cache hit, it returns the value directly.
Nothing is scheduled, and no thread changes.
A paused coroutine costs one object, not a thread stack.
That is why you can have hundreds of thousands.
And plain code cannot call a suspend function.
It has no continuation to pass in.
